topicData.topic: Focus the post on Apple’s leadership transition from Tim Cook to John Ternus and the deeper operating-model question it creates. Cook built one of the most disciplined and successful operating machines in corporate history, but Ternus may now need to challenge parts of that same model as AI changes the basis of competition. The core idea: the hardest companies to transform are often the ones whose existing model has worked exceptionally well. Make it a leadership and organisational transformation story, not a generic Apple or AI post.
topicData.angle: Write from the specific details and your honest reaction to this topic.

postText:
The hardest transformation isn't fixing a broken company. It's convincing a wildly successful one that its own model has become the risk.

That's what John Ternus actually inherits.

Tim Cook didn't just build a strategy. He built a belief system. Supply chain discipline as competitive moat. Hardware margins as the measure of winning. Precision at a scale most organisations never get close to. And it worked so well, for so long, that every internal instinct now points in one direction. Protect the model.

That's the trap.

AI doesn't care how beautifully your operations run. It shifts what actually wins. The organisations I've watched struggle most with this aren't the broken ones. They're the ones that got exceptionally good at something, got rewarded for it repeatedly, and now carry that success as a kind of weight. Every decision gets filtered through a logic that used to be right.

I've seen the same pattern in telecoms operators sitting on years of infrastructure investment, and in facilities management firms whose entire margin model depends on labour optimisation that AI is starting to eat from below. The instinct is identical. And it makes sense. You don't dismantle what made you.

But Ternus's real job isn't engineering. It's helping Apple work through a model it still loves, while competitors are already operating on different assumptions.

That's genuinely hard. Not strategically hard. Humanly hard.

The people around him built careers inside that belief system. The incentives still reward it. The numbers still mostly justify it. And he has to stand in front of all of that and make the case for a different logic before the market makes it for him.

I don't know if he gets there. I'm not sure anyone on the outside can tell yet.

But I'd be watching less for what Apple announces on AI, and more for whether the internal operating model starts to shift beneath it. That's where the real signal will be.

What does leadership succession look like in your organisation when the incoming leader needs to challenge the very model that made the outgoing one successful?
